toc.title: Encryption in Transit or Before Transit (skill 4.3.4)

html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. KMS: Key Management Service; GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation; PII: personally identifiable information; EBS: Elastic Block Store; IAM: Identity and Access Management; SSE: server-side encryption; DSSE: dual-layer server-side encryption; RDS: Relational Database Service; EMR: Elastic MapReduce; EMRFS: EMR File System; EFS: Elastic File System; ACM: AWS Certificate Manager; VPC: Virtual Private Cloud; SDK: software development kit; MFA: multi-factor authentication; DDM: dynamic data masking

  • Mask and anonymize data according to compliance laws or company policy
  • Use encryption keys (AWS KMS) to encrypt and decrypt data
  • Configure encryption across AWS account boundaries
  • Enable encryption in transit or before transit

2Masking and Anonymization (skill 4.3.1)

Running case

Kestrel Freight Protects Customer Data

  • Test teams need realistic data but not real names and phone numbers
  • Analysts need trends by customer, but not who the customer is
  • A privacy law limits how personal data may be stored and shared
  • Your job: keep the value of the data and remove the risk
Technique What it does Reversible? Use it for
Masking (static) Replaces values with fake or partial ones (****-1234) in a copy No Test and development data
Dynamic masking Hides or partly shows values at query time by role; stored data unchanged Yes (for authorized roles) Redshift dynamic data masking
Redaction Removes the value No Free text, logs
Hashing One-way fingerprint of a value; the same input gives the same hash No Joining on a masked key, matching without revealing
Tokenization Replaces the value with a token; the real value lives in a secure vault Yes, with the vault Payment data, IDs
Pseudonymization Replaces identifiers with a pseudonym; a key or table can re-identify Yes Analytics that must link records
Anonymization Irreversibly removes the link to a person (generalize, aggregate, suppress, add noise) No Sharing data publicly; data that falls outside privacy law when truly anonymous
Generalization Reduce precision (age 34 → 30–39, full address → region) No Statistics
  • Pseudonymized data is still personal data under many laws (for example the GDPR) because it can be re-identified; truly anonymized data is not
  • Choose by need: analysis needs joins → hash or pseudonym; testing → static mask; role-based viewing → dynamic masking or column permissions; sharing externally → anonymize

AWS tools

Need Tool
Find personal data Amazon Macie (S3), Glue detect-PII transform, Amazon Comprehend (text)
Mask or hash columns in a pipeline AWS Glue DataBrew (mask, hash, encrypt, shuffle, substitute), AWS Glue ETL (PII detection and redaction), Lambda
Show masked values to some users Redshift dynamic data masking, Lake Formation column and row filters (Module 15), views
Protect model prompts and outputs Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (filters sensitive information)
Exam tip

"Give developers realistic test data with no real personal data" → mask or substitute in a copy (DataBrew or Glue). "Show the last four digits to support staff only" → dynamic data masking.

3Encryption Keys with AWS KMS (skill 4.3.2)

  • AWS Key Management Service (KMS) creates and controls encryption keys; keys never leave KMS unencrypted; every use is logged in CloudTrail
  • Key types:
Type Who manages Notes
AWS owned key AWS (not visible) Free; no control or audit
AWS managed key (aws/s3, aws/redshift...) AWS for your account Rotated every year; fixed key policy
Customer managed key (CMK) You Your key policy, rotation choice, can be used across accounts, can be disabled or scheduled for deletion; charged per key
  • Symmetric keys (one key to encrypt and decrypt, default) and asymmetric keys (public and private pair: signing and encryption outside AWS)
  • Envelope encryption: KMS encrypts only small data keys (GenerateDataKey); the data key encrypts the large data; this is how S3, EBS, Redshift and others use KMS
  • Access control: the key policy is the primary control (IAM policies work only if the key policy allows IAM); grants give temporary, specific permission to AWS services; permissions are separate for kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt, kms:GenerateDataKey
  • Rotation: for customer managed keys, automatic rotation (every 365 days by default, with a custom period option, plus on-demand rotation) keeps the same key ID; old key material is kept so old data stays readable [Verify live]
  • Deletion: a waiting period of 7 to 30 days before a key is deleted; data encrypted under a deleted key is unrecoverable

Encryption at rest in the data services

Service At rest
Amazon S3 SSE-S3 on every new object by default; SSE-KMS (your key, audit trail; bucket keys cut KMS request cost); DSSE-KMS (two layers); SSE-C (your key, supplied per request; disabled by default on new buckets [Verify live]); client-side
Amazon Redshift KMS-encrypted clusters and snapshots (Redshift Serverless is always encrypted)
Amazon RDS / Aurora KMS, chosen at creation (to encrypt an unencrypted database, copy a snapshot with encryption and restore)
Amazon DynamoDB Always encrypted at rest; choose AWS owned, AWS managed or customer managed key
AWS Glue Security configurations encrypt S3 targets, CloudWatch logs and job bookmarks
Kinesis Data Streams / Firehose Server-side encryption with KMS
Amazon EMR Security configuration: at-rest (S3 EMRFS, local disks, EBS) and in-transit options
Athena Encrypt query results in S3 per workgroup
Amazon EBS / EFS KMS
Exam tip

"Control the key, audit every use, and be able to disable access quickly" → SSE-KMS with a customer managed key. "Cut the KMS request cost of an S3-heavy pipeline" → S3 Bucket Keys.

4Encryption across Account Boundaries (skill 4.3.3)

  • Two permissions are needed: the key policy (in the key's account) must allow the other account (or role), and an IAM policy in the other account must allow its role to use that key
  • Use a customer managed key for anything shared: AWS managed keys and AWS owned keys cannot be shared with another account
  • Typical cases:
    • S3 objects encrypted with SSE-KMS read by another account: bucket policy (or access point) allows the principal and the key policy allows kms:Decrypt
    • Sharing an encrypted RDS or Redshift snapshot: encrypt with a customer managed key, share the snapshot, and share the key with the other account; the recipient copies the snapshot and re-encrypts with its own key
    • Lake Formation or Redshift data sharing across accounts: grant on the data and allow the key
    • Replication to another account or Region: allow KMS on both keys
  • Grants and conditions: use kms:ViaService (only through S3), encryption context, and organization conditions to limit use
Exam tip

"Another account cannot read objects in a shared bucket that use SSE-KMS" → add the account to the CMK's key policy and kms:Decrypt to its role; an AWS managed key cannot be shared.

5Encryption in Transit or Before Transit (skill 4.3.4)

  • In transit = while moving: use TLS (HTTPS); AWS service APIs use TLS; enforce it:
    • S3: a bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SecureTransport is false (and can require a minimum TLS version)
    • Redshift: set require_ssl in the parameter group; RDS/Aurora: require SSL (for example rds.force_ssl for PostgreSQL)
    • Kafka (MSK) and Kinesis: TLS in transit; EMR: in-transit encryption options
    • API Gateway and load balancers: HTTPS with ACM certificates
  • Private paths reduce exposure: VPC endpoints and PrivateLink, Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec), Direct Connect (private, encrypt with VPN or MACsec if required)
  • Before transit (client-side encryption): encrypt on the source before sending, so only ciphertext travels and is stored; the service never sees plaintext: AWS Encryption SDK, S3 encryption client, DynamoDB encryption client; keys come from KMS (GenerateDataKey)
  • Choose: TLS is the baseline; client-side encryption for the highest control (AWS cannot read the data) at the cost of key handling and less service-side processing (the service cannot query encrypted values)
Exam tip

"Make sure no one can upload or read over HTTP" → bucket policy denying aws:SecureTransport = false. "AWS must never see plaintext" → client-side encryption.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Kestrel Freight's developers need realistic test data without any real customer names or phone numbers. What is the best approach?

  • ACopy the production data to the test account without any change
  • BGive the developers read access to the production tables directly
  • CEncrypt the production data with SSE-S3 and share the encrypted files
  • DCreate a masked or substituted copy of the data with Glue DataBrew or a Glue job
Show the answer

Answer: D. Static masking or substitution in a copy keeps realistic structure while removing personal data. Encryption does not remove personal data from authorized readers.

S2An S3 bucket in account A holds objects encrypted with SSE-KMS under a customer managed key. A role in account B cannot read them even though the bucket policy allows it. Which TWO actions fix this? (Select TWO.)

  • AAdd account B (or its role) to the KMS key policy
  • BRemove encryption from the bucket
  • CSwitch the objects to an AWS managed key and share it
  • DDisable CloudTrail
  • EAllow kms:Decrypt on that key in the role's IAM policy in account B
Show the answer

Answer: A, E. Cross-account KMS use needs permission in the key policy and in the caller's IAM policy. AWS managed keys cannot be shared.

S3A team must ensure that no client can send or retrieve S3 data over unencrypted connections. What should be configured?

  • AA bucket policy that denies requests when aws:SecureTransport is false
  • BS3 Versioning enabled with MFA delete on the bucket and a lifecycle rule for old versions
  • CAn S3 Lifecycle rule that expires objects that are not encrypted
  • DS3 Replication to a second bucket in the same Region
Show the answer

Answer: A. The aws:SecureTransport condition identifies requests made over HTTP, which the policy denies.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Masking techniques Static mask (copy), dynamic mask (query time, by role), redact, hash (one-way), tokenize (vault), pseudonymize (reversible; still personal data), anonymize (irreversible), generalize
Tools Macie / Glue detect-PII / Comprehend to find; DataBrew / Glue to mask; Redshift DDM / Lake Formation filters / views to show by role; Bedrock Guardrails
KMS keys AWS owned, AWS managed (yearly rotation, fixed policy), customer managed (your policy, rotation, shareable, 7–30 day deletion wait); symmetric default; envelope encryption
KMS access Key policy first; IAM works only if the key policy allows it; grants for services; kms:Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey
At rest S3 SSE-S3 default, SSE-KMS (+ bucket keys), DSSE-KMS, SSE-C; Redshift/RDS/DynamoDB/Kinesis/Glue/EMR/Athena all KMS-capable; RDS encryption at creation
Cross-account Customer managed key; key policy + IAM policy; AWS managed keys cannot be shared; share encrypted snapshots with the key
In transit TLS everywhere; aws:SecureTransport, Redshift require_ssl, RDS force SSL; VPC endpoints / VPN / Direct Connect (+MACsec); client-side encryption (AWS Encryption SDK) for plaintext-never-leaves
